query: Earlier W-based high-entropy alloys showed promising microstructural stability, high-temperature strength, and irradiation tolerance, but most contained Nb, Mo, Cr, or Ni, whose activation behavior and other service limitations restrict their suitability for plasma-facing components. Candidate structural materials must combine thermal and mechanical performance with low neutron activation and rapid radioactive decay. The equimolar WTaTiVZr alloy uses refractory, relatively low-activation constituents and has shown creep and molten-salt-corrosion resistance, yet its plastic strain and toughness remain unreported and poorly understood. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs its plastic strain and toughness relative to commercially used pure tungsten under high-temperature plasma-facing-component service? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the hypothesized cause, the observations predicted relative to pure tungsten, the boundaries of validity, the cited prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In equimolar WTaTiVZr, the severe local lattice distortions from random atomic mixing destabilize the narrow screw dislocation cores typical of BCC tungsten and instead promote the activation and glide of <111>{110} edge dislocations. This shift in dominant dislocation mechanism reduces the Peierls barrier for dislocation motion at high temperatures, thereby increasing plastic strain capability and toughness relative to pure tungsten.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, single-phase equimolar WTaTiVZr refractory high‐entropy alloy exhibiting significant lattice distortion.
generation.intervention: High‐temperature mechanical testing (e.g., tensile or creep tests) under plasma‐facing-component service conditions (800–900 °C) comparing equimolar WTaTiVZr with commercially used pure tungsten.
generation.conditions: Identical thermal and loading conditions in an inert atmosphere (to avoid oxidation), using specimens of similar geometry and processing history to isolate the effect of alloy composition.
generation.structural_mediator: The random atomic size and bonding variations generating local lattice distortions that modify dislocation core structures.
generation.mechanism: The compositional randomness causes pronounced lattice distortions, which broaden dislocation cores and diminish the traditional dominance of screw dislocations that have high Peierls barriers in pure tungsten. Instead, less temperature‐sensitive <111>{110} edge dislocations are activated, which can glide and multiply more readily at high temperatures. This results in better strain accommodation and energy dissipation during deformation, leading to improved toughness and plastic strain.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to pure tungsten, the WTaTiVZr alloy will exhibit a lower apparent yield strength but significantly enhanced ductility and toughness at high temperatures, along with microstructural evidence (via TEM or neutron diffraction) of a higher proportion of mobile edge dislocations compared to the predominantly sluggish screw dislocations in tungsten.
generation.baseline: Commercial pure tungsten, which under high temperatures shows limited plastic deformation and poor toughness due to its reliance on high-barrier, screw dislocation-mediated plasticity.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for equimolar WTaTiVZr alloys with a homogeneous BCC structure and under high-temperature plasma-facing conditions (approximately 800–900 °C). Deviations may occur if secondary phases or significant precipitates form, or if service conditions deviate substantially from the test environment.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of improvement in plastic strain and toughness is uncertain and may depend on processing history and microstructural uniformity. Additionally, effects from irradiation or surface phenomena under actual plasma service conditions remain to be fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: equimolar WTaTiVZr alloy and high-purity tungsten, processed into identical specimen geometries. Subject both sets to high-temperature tensile and creep tests (e.g., at 800–900 °C) in an inert atmosphere. Use in situ TEM or neutron diffraction to monitor dislocation activity during deformation.
measurements: Stress-strain curves including yield strength, total elongation, and fracture toughness
In situ imaging and diffraction analyses to identify the dominant dislocation types (edge versus screw)
Fracture surface analysis for ductile versus brittle features
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the WTaTiVZr alloy does not show demonstrably higher plastic strain and toughness, or if dislocation analysis reveals no significant increase in mobile edge dislocations relative to pure tungsten under identical high-temperature conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

System: Nb23.8Ta25.5Ti24.9V25.8 (nominally Nb25Ta25Ti25V25) BCC refractory high-entropy alloy. Processing: Arc melting under argon atmosphere from 99.99 wt% purity elements, melted 10 times, drop-cast into 4-mm diameter rods, homogenized at 1200°C for 3 days, followed by water cooling.
